## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Surāghaṭajātaka* (Ja 291), also known under the title *Bhadraghaṭajātaka* and translated as "The Lucky Cup" or "Protecting Good Fortune", is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010]. According to its framing narrative, the Buddha recounted the story at Jetavana regarding a nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika [SuttaCentral]. The nephew lived recklessly and died wretchedly by the city wall; when Anāthapiṇḍika asked whether he could have prevented his nephew's demise, the Buddha explained that the nephew belonged to that group of insatiable people who resemble bottomless vats and had met ruin through his own reckless habits in a past life as well [Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is identified as the deity Sakka, who comes to the aid of a destitute man who had been his son in a previous existence by giving him a wishing-cup or miraculous jar that provides whatever he needs [Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010]. However, the dissolute fellow uses it to get drunk, carelessly breaks the jar, and is reduced to poverty once again [Anandajoti 2010]. The accompanying canonical verse moralizes that while a low person quickly becomes drunk even on poor drinks, the virtuous person remains sober even after drinking the finest liquor [Anandajoti 2010].

DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse with the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo, §§1.1–3.4) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also registers automated cross-language textual alignments with Tibetan translations of the *Gurulekha* (D4186) and the *Udānavarga* (D4099) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral lists four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
